title: Runtime isolation & noisy-neighbor technical deep dive
topics: quantization impact on throughput and quality
dedicated vs hosted isolation strategies and SLAs
summary: Redwood SE walked HelixCloud through microbenchmarks comparing hosted vs dedicated setups focusing on noisy-neighbor scenarios. Key takeaways: dedicated gives strong isolation for throughput and predictable latency under high concurrency; hosted relies on smart routing, burst pools, and fallback model variants for resilience. KV cache and prefix caching significantly reduce p99 when locality is high; batching improves throughput but needs adaptive cutoff to protect tail latency. Quantization (int8/fp16) yields 1.9-2.8x throughput at small quality cost for our test prompts; recommended pilot on dedicated with KPS profiling.

Schedule a 2-hour lab session to run Helix-specific workload (Devon + Sana)
Send VPC architecture diagram and security/SSO checklist (Priya)

transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-05-21
- Start: 15:30 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Avery Collins (Redwood AE), Devon Nguyen (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood SRE), Marcus Li (Helix Platform Eng), Sana Ortega (Helix ML Infra), Robert Chen (Helix CTO)

Summary/Notes (auto): quick perf deep dive, noisy neighbor repros, recommended pilot on Dedicated with quantization/kv-cache tuning

[00:00] Avery Collins: All right, hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're about 60 minutes on this deep dive, the goal is to go through the noisy neighbor and isolation patterns and then map that back to a pilot plan. Devon, you want to kick off with the microbench results?

[00:22] Devon Nguyen: Yeah sure. Hi Marcus, Sana — quick context: we ran three workloads: bursty chat, steady throughput embeddings, and mixed inference with large context. For each we compared Hosted (multi-tenant with routing + autoscale) and Dedicated (reserved GPU pool). I have slides but I'll just read the key numbers for now — p50/p95/p99 differ a lot under contention.

[00:41] Marcus Li: Sorry can you clarify "dedicated pool" means full gpu tenancy per customer or shared but reserved capacity?

[00:48] Devon Nguyen: Good question — dedicated in our terms is reserved GPU nodes where the inference runtime and model copies are isolated to your tenant. There can still be multiple models per node but compute scheduling is only for your org — so noisy neighbor from other tenants is eliminated.

[01:05] Sana Ortega: And for hosted, how do you guarantee throughput? We care about 99% latency under heavy bursts — our SLAs are strict.

[01:12] Devon Nguyen: Hosted relies on smart routing. We keep hot-replica caches, prefix/KV cache to speed up repeated tokens, and adaptive batching. When a zone is strained we route to a compatible model variant or different region. That keeps things online but latency may spike to the p99 unless you use Dedicated.

[01:34] Robert Chen: Is the routing automatic or does it require us to change client code?

[01:39] Avery Collins: It's transparent. The API surface is the same — you can pin model versions but routing fallback is managed by Redwood's control plane. You can also set policies: strict (no fallback) or permissive (allow smaller/quantized variants).

[01:55] Devon Nguyen: Back to microbench: for high concurrency bursts (1000 concurrent short chats), Hosted p99 moved from 420ms baseline to 1.6s under noisy neighbor injection. Dedicated stayed around 430-520ms. The main difference was KV cache hit rate — Dedicated had higher cache locality because there was no eviction pressure from other tenants.

[02:20] Marcus Li: How did you simulate noisy neighbor? We run a lot of background embeddings and batch jobs during our run windows.

[02:25] Devon Nguyen: We launched synthetic workloads that saturated GPU memory and copy bandwidth — large-batch embeddings at 512 batch-size on a shared pool, while the chat workload had small reqs. We also artificially fragmented GPU memory to stress allocator. The noisy neighbor effect shows as KV eviction and kernel scheduling latency.

[02:45] Sana Ortega: You mentioned KV cache; is that on-host or external? We have concerns about data residency and that caching might keep sensitive prefixes in memory.

[02:54] Priya Shah: Good point; our KV cache for Hosted runs in the same runtime process and is ephemeral — it does not persist to disk. For Private/VPC we can route cache to a customer-managed memcached/redis inside the VPC if needed, or we scope the cache lifetime and disable prefix caching for certain routes. We'll document options.

[03:16] Marcus Li: For Dedicated, do we get the option to co-locate the KV store in our VPC?

[03:20] Priya Shah: Yes, for Redwood Private/Dedicated-with-VPC you can have the cache endpoint inside your VPC. That reduces cross-region hops and meets data residency. There's an integration doc we'll share.

[03:33] [Slide change noise] Devon Nguyen: Next, batching. We tested continuous batching and burst-adaptive cutoff. Pure aggressive batching gave 2.6x throughput on throughput tests but increased median by ~10-30ms and p99 could balloon if the adaptive cutoff mispredicted queue arrival. So our recommendation: enable batching with a strict max latency budget per route and let the runtime drop into small-batch mode when tail approaches SLO.

[03:58] Sana Ortega: In practice, how do you set that latency budget? We have mixed SLAs across endpoints.

[04:03] Devon Nguyen: You configure per-route SLO in the console — the runtime will use a PID-style controller to keep batching sizes within that latency. For experimentation you can set a hard cutoff 100ms or 200ms depending on your tolerance. We'll help tune.

[04:17] Marcus Li: Quantization — what's the impact on quality? We run some sensitive summarization tasks.

[04:22] Devon Nguyen: We ran int8 and fp16 quant knobs on models similar to the ones you described. Throughput improved roughly 1.9x for fp16 and up to 2.8x for int8 in our kernels with per-layer calibration. Quality regressions were small for retrieval and chitchat, but some edge-case summarization prompts had token-level shift ~0.4-1.7 perplexity delta — perceptible in strict summarization. Our suggestion: pilot quantized variants on Dedicated where you can run A/B and fallback to full-precision if quality drops.

[04:52] Robert Chen: So Dedicated lets us do A/B at the routing layer?

[04:55] Avery Collins: Yes, rollouts are independent of infra: you can do canary on a quantized endpoint and fail over automatically. The difference is that Dedicated gives stable perf characteristics so the A/B metrics are less noisy.

[05:08] Marcus Li: Network — our infra sits behind a VPC and we use private peering. How much network latency should we expect for on-prem or VPC deployments versus hosted?

[05:17] Priya Shah: For a VPC deployment in the same region, additional network latency is typically 2-12ms round-trip depending on peering and paths. On-prem with a cross-datacenter link can be 10-40ms. Those numbers matter for short 20-80 token calls where network dominates. For heavy-token runs, GPU time dominates. So we'll include those estimates in the benchmark sheet.

[05:40] Sana Ortega: Do you support HSM/KMS for key management in Private? We need customer-managed keys to satisfy our compliance.

[05:46] Priya Shah: Yes — KMS/HSM integrations are available for Private deployments and for Dedicated we can integrate with your KMS in VPC. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption with Redwood-managed keys or customer-managed keys in supported clouds. We'll attach the security checklist.

[06:00] Devon Nguyen: Back to the noisy neighbor mitigation techniques: we instrument kernel preemption, cgroup limits for CPU and io, and we queue requests into per-tenant queues. For Hosted we also do opportunistic pre-warming and cold-start mitigations via model warm pools. But when neighbors create high device memory pressure, eviction of KV and forcing recompute is the main cause of p99 spikes.

[06:24] Marcus Li: Can you throttle the noisy workloads in Hosted if they're causing interference? Like embeddings that run off-schedule?

[06:29] Avery Collins: We have policy controls — you can create QoS tiers and set token/call quotas per API key. For customer-supplied APIs we recommend isolating heavy batch jobs to off-peak windows or to Dedicated capacity.

[06:45] Robert Chen: Is there a difference in cost efficiency between dedicated and hosted when you factor in these buffers for noisy neighbor?

[06:50] Devon Nguyen: Hosted can be cost-efficient at low-to-medium utilization because we multi-tenant and share model parameters. Dedicated is more predictable: you pay for reserved GPUs but you get steady throughput. For heavy sustained inference Dedicated often wins on unit cost because you can tune quantization and batching more aggressively without noisy neighbors. We'll run a cost-per-token calc for your load profile.

[07:12] Marcus Li: About kernel selection and compilation — do you recompile kernels per tenant or is that shared? We run custom ops occasionally.

[07:19] Devon Nguyen: Kernels are selected at runtime, and we cache compilation artifacts. In Dedicated or Private you can permit custom kernels; those artifacts live within your control plane/cluster and do not mingle with other tenants. For Hosted we maintain a curated set of optimized kernels; custom ops would be a Private conversation.

[07:36] [Crosstalk] Sana Ortega: A quick question about metrics — will we get token-level traces and KV hit rates in the console?

[07:42] Priya Shah: Yes, Redwood Console exposes token latency histograms, KV hit/miss rates, batch size distributions, and per-model counters. We can also stream traces to your observability stack.

[07:55] Marcus Li: On failure modes — if a node OOMs on Dedicated what happens to requests in-flight?

[08:01] Devon Nguyen: We have a per-node preemption policy: the runtime tries to gracefully reject single requests that would blow memory, with a 429/503 and retry hint. For Dedicated we also include automatic restart policies and optional warm standby replicas if you opt for multi-AZ Dedicated. For Hosted we prefer live migration and cross-zone failover. We can show logs of the rejections from our tests.

[08:21] Robert Chen: How do you recommend we structure the pilot? We want realistic production loads, including off-hour batch jobs.

[08:28] Avery Collins: Suggested pilot: 2-week Dedicated reservation of 4x A100-ish GPUs, replay a week's worth of traffic including daily batch windows, run quantized and full-precision variants, and collect p50/p95/p99, KV hit rates, batch sizes, and cost-per-token. We'll run the first half with default runtime settings and second half with tuned batching and cache params.

[08:46] Marcus Li: That sounds good. For the replay — can we feed in our event logs? We prefer not to send raw PII to external systems.

[08:53] Priya Shah: You can run the replay inside your VPC with Redwood Private, or we can sign a limited processing agreement for the pilot. Also we can redact sensitive fields in flight; we have transforms.

[09:06] Sana Ortega: Quick nit: earlier you mentioned model variants for fallback. Are those quantized variants or smaller-arch models?

[09:12] Devon Nguyen: Both. Fallback tiers can be quantized versions, distilled smaller-architecture variants, or even cached outputs for common prompts. You can control which tiers are allowed per route.

[09:24] Marcus Li: For our use case, we need deterministic p99 under 600ms for 8k tokens average session length — is that realistic on Dedicated?

[09:32] Devon Nguyen: 8k tokens is large — GPU compute dominates. On a 4x A100 dedicated pool with tuned quantization and batching we observed median ~400ms and p99 ~700-800ms for 8k token generation in our synthetic — so you're close. We need to run your exact model and prompts to make a call. The pilot will tell.

[09:53] Robert Chen: Do you have any runbook recommendations to prevent noisy neighbor impact if we pick Hosted?

[09:59] Avery Collins: Yes: 1) segregate large batch jobs into different API keys and schedule off-peak, 2) use per-route SLO and hard fallbacks, 3) enable prefix/KV cache with scoped lifetimes, 4) set quotas for embeddings endpoints to avoid sudden saturation. We'll include a runbook doc.

[10:18] [Pause — background keyboard]

[10:25] Devon Nguyen: One more micro detail — KV cache semantics: we use a combination of LRU and size-aware eviction. In Hosted the eviction rate under contention rose to 45% which led to re-tokenization/computation; in Dedicated it dropped to 8-12%. That correlates strongly with p99 regressions. So cache sizing and locality of workload (many repeated sessions) is important.

[10:48] Sana Ortega: Can we set sticky routing to improve locality? We have many sessions per user across time.

[10:53] Devon Nguyen: Yes you can enable session affinity at the API key level so requests for that session go to the same runtime bucket to improve cache hit. That's supported in Dedicated and optionally in Hosted with caveats around autoscaling.

[11:06] Marcus Li: Any gotchas with quantization on long-context models? We've seen some hallucination/syntax shifts.

[11:12] Devon Nguyen: Long contexts amplify small representational errors. Our per-layer calibration and mixed-precision pipelines mitigate a lot but some prompts are sensitive. For long-context generation we typically recommend fp16 or mixed int8-fp16 hybrid where we quantize only attention and keep critical layers in fp16. That gives throughput while maintaining coherence.

[11:34] Robert Chen: Is live rollback instantaneous if we detect quality drift?

[11:37] Avery Collins: Rollback at routing layer is near-instant; you can configure automatic rollback triggers based on eval metrics or manual. The push itself is fast since it's traffic-routing rather than model load.

[11:46] Devon Nguyen: A small note on telemetry: for the pilot we'll surface per-request debug logs (sampling) so your team can correlate failures to model variant, kernel selection, KV hit/miss. That helped our internal teams root cause noisy neighbor regressions.

[12:03] Sana Ortega: Will that sampling have PII? We need control.

[12:07] Priya Shah: Sampling can be redacted and you can set filters — we'll provide the controls.

[12:15] Marcus Li: Ok let's recap next steps briefly.

[12:18] Avery Collins: Sure — Redwood will: share benchmark spreadsheet and runbook (Devon), provide VPC/private architecture diagrams and security checklist (Priya), set up a 2-week Dedicated pilot quote (Avery). Helix will: confirm GPU procurement and pilot window (Marcus), provide sample workload logs or a sanitized replay (Sana). We'll schedule the lab session for week of 2025-06-02.

[12:42] Robert Chen: I want to read that spreadsheet before committing budget. Is there a quick cost estimate?

[12:47] Avery Collins: We'll include an estimated cost-per-token and projected monthly cost at the pilot utilization. Expect a ballpark in the spreadsheet but we'll discuss precise numbers once we have the workload replay.

[12:58] Marcus Li: Perfect. Quick question: any legal/compliance friction with Dedicated + VPC? We do need SOC2 plus customer-managed keys.

[13:06] Priya Shah: Dedicated with VPC meets SOC2 and we support CMKs. We'll attach the compliance packet. For Private on-prem we can do air-gapped deployments but that adds delivery lead time.

[13:20] Avery Collins: Anything else from the team?

[13:23] Sana Ortega: No, that's it. Thanks — excited to run the pilot.

[13:27] Marcus Li: Thanks everyone.

[13:30] [Meeting end]

Notes on transcript quality: auto transcription had a few mislabels and some technical terms mangled (e.g., "k v cash" instead of KV), timestamps sampled ~every 20-90s.
